CH_People.name: Augustus
CH_People.description: First Roman emperor, reigning during the birth of Jesus. Established the Pax Romana. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus

CH_People.name: Tiberius
CH_People.description: Emperor during the ministry and crucifixion of Jesus. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius

CH_People.name: Claudius
CH_People.description: Expelled Jews from Rome (Acts 18:2). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudius

CH_People.name: Galba, Otho & Aulus Vitellius
CH_People.description: Year of the Four Emperors — civil war following Nero's death. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_of_the_Four_Emperors

CH_People.name: Vespasian
CH_People.description: Founded the Flavian dynasty; commanded the siege of Jerusalem in 70 AD before becoming emperor. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vespasian

CH_People.name: Caligula
CH_People.description: Briefly reigned; known for erratic and tyrannical behavior. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula

CH_People.name: Nerva
CH_People.description: First of the Five Good Emperors; adopted Trajan as successor. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nerva

CH_People.name: Nero
CH_People.description: Blamed Christians for the Great Fire of Rome (64 AD); first major imperial persecutor of Christians. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nero

CH_People.name: Titus
CH_People.description: As general, destroyed the Second Temple in Jerusalem (70 AD). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titus

CH_People.name: Cerinthus
CH_People.description: An early gnostic teacher who held that the Christ descended on the man Jesus at his baptism and left him before the crucifixion. Irenaeus reports that John the Apostle wrote against him. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerinthus

CH_People.name: Domitian
CH_People.description: Persecuted Christians late in his reign; tradition links him to the exile of John to Patmos. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domitian

CH_People.name: Trajan
CH_People.description: Under his rule the empire reached its greatest territorial extent. Corresponded with Pliny about treatment of Christians. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trajan

CH_People.name: Papias of Hieropolis
CH_People.description: Eusebius' quotations of Papias are all that survive of Papias' works. It is in these that he is quoted as describing Mark's gospel as the faithful recording of Peter's account of the life, death and resurrection of Jesus. (Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, 2nd Ed., 1993)

CH_People.name: Hadrian
CH_People.description: Rebuilt Jerusalem as Aelia Capitolina, triggering the Bar Kokhba revolt. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadrian

CH_People.name: Basilides
CH_People.description: Alexandrian gnostic teacher, among the earliest named systematisers of gnostic cosmology. Known chiefly through the refutations of Irenaeus and Hippolytus. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilides

CH_People.name: Marcion of Sinope
CH_People.description: Taught that the God of the Hebrew scriptures was a lesser deity distinct from the Father of Jesus, and produced the first known Christian canon by cutting Luke and ten Pauline letters free of the Old Testament. Excommunicated at Rome in 144. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcion_of_Sinope

CH_People.name: Antoninus Pius
CH_People.description: Longest-reigning of the Five Good Emperors; a period of relative peace for Christians. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoninus_Pius

CH_People.name: Valentinus
CH_People.description: The most influential gnostic teacher of the second century, who nearly became bishop of Rome. His school prompted Irenaeus' Against Heresies. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentinus_(Gnostic)

CH_People.name: Tatian
CH_People.description:
"Our doctrines are older, not only than those of the Greeks, but than the invention of letters." -Tatian (Pelikan, Jaroslav. The Christian Tradition: The Development of Christian Doctrine, Vol. 1., 35)

Described as the "pupil of Justin Martyr", but also as a the "literary opponent" of  Irenaeus, Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, Hippolytus and Origen. (Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, 2nd. Ed., 1993).

CH_People.name: Marcus Aurelius
CH_People.description: Stoic philosopher-emperor. Persecution of Christians occurred during his reign, including the martyrdom of Polycarp. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Aurelius

CH_People.name: Montanus
CH_People.description: Founder of the New Prophecy, an ecstatic prophetic movement in Phrygia promising continuing revelation and rigorous discipline. Tertullian joined it late in life. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montanus

CH_People.name: Septimius Severus
CH_People.description: Founded the Severan dynasty. His wife Julia Domna was sympathetic to various religions. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Septimius_Severus

CH_People.name: Commodus
CH_People.description: Last of the Antonine dynasty; his misrule led to the Crisis of the Third Century. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commodus

CH_People.name: Maximinus Thrax
CH_People.description: First soldier-emperor; targeted Christian clergy, initiating a brief persecution. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximinus_Thrax

CH_People.name: Sabellius
CH_People.description: Taught that Father, Son and Spirit are three modes or roles of a single divine person rather than three persons — the position that gave modalism its other name, Sabellianism. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabellius

CH_People.name: Caracalla
CH_People.description: Extended Roman citizenship to all free inhabitants of the empire (Constitutio Antoniniana). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caracalla

CH_People.name: Valerian
CH_People.description: Persecuted Christians; captured alive by the Sasanian king Shapur I — the only Roman emperor taken prisoner. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valerian_(emperor)

CH_People.name: Novatian
CH_People.description: Roman presbyter and able trinitarian theologian who, holding that those who lapsed under persecution could not be readmitted, was set up as a rival bishop of Rome against Cornelius in 251. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novatian

CH_People.name: Paul of Samosata
CH_People.description: Bishop of Antioch deposed by the Synod of Antioch in 268 for teaching that Christ was a mere man on whom the Word rested — an adoptionist monarchianism. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_of_Samosata

CH_People.name: Decius
CH_People.description: Ordered empire-wide sacrifice to Roman gods, launching the Decian persecution of Christians. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decius

CH_People.name: Philip the Arab
CH_People.description: Some ancient sources claim he was the first Christian emperor; celebrated Rome's millennium. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_the_Arab

CH_People.name: Alexander Severus
CH_People.description: Tolerant of Christians; his household reportedly included images of Christ alongside other religious figures. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Severus

CH_People.name: Gregory Thaumaturgus
CH_People.description:
"The wealth of legends and miracles which were attributed to him in later times and to which he owes his surname of Thaumaturgus or wonder-worker, such as the moving of a mountain and the drying-up of a swamp, testify to his uncommon strength of character as well as to his popularity...In 264-265 he took part in the first Synod of Antioch against Paul of Samosata; he also fought Sabellianism and Tritheism." (Oxfort Dictionary of the Christian Church, 2nd ed., 1993)

Note: Gregory Thaumaturgus was thought to have died between 270 and 275. I have given him a later death here because Gregory of Nazianzus, and Basil the Great state that he instructed Macrina the Elder, their grandmother - who was born shortly before 270. I'm also revising Macrina the Elder's birth year to be 260.

CH_People.name: Aurelian
CH_People.description: Reunited the empire after the Crisis of the Third Century. Promoted the cult of Sol Invictus. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurelian

CH_People.name: Mani
CH_People.description: Persian prophet whose dualist religion of light and darkness spread across the empire and held the young Augustine for nine years. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mani_(prophet)

CH_People.name: Gallienus
CH_People.description: Ended his father Valerian's persecution and issued an edict of toleration for Christians. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallienus

CH_People.name: Diocletian/Maximian
CH_People.description: Established the Tetrarchy. Launched the Great Persecution (303–311), the last and most severe persecution of Christians in the empire. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocletian

CH_People.name: Lucian of Antioch
CH_People.description: Lucian was possibly connected with Arius and Paul of Samosata, but despite what his earlier views may have been, he died as a martyr and is venerated by both the Catholic and the Orthodox church.-MB

CH_People.name: Anthony the Great
CH_People.description: Considered one of the fathers of monasticism, Anthony was part of the spiritual exodus into the desert from the cities during a period of decline. An early biography was written by Athanasius of Alexandria: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/2811.htm

CH_People.name: Arius
CH_People.description: Alexandrian presbyter who taught that the Son was a creature, made out of nothing before time — "there was when he was not." Condemned at Nicaea in 325, but the controversy he began ran for another sixty years. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arius

CH_People.name: Ossius of Córdoba
CH_People.description: Constantine's ecclesiastical adviser, who presided at Nicaea and is widely credited with pressing the word homoousios into the creed. Broken at the very end by Constantius II, aged over a hundred. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hosius_of_Corduba

CH_People.name: Eusebius of Caesarea
CH_People.description: The first church historian, and a subordinationist who was provisionally excommunicated before Nicaea and signed the creed with evident reluctance. Indispensable as a source, unreliable as a witness to his own party. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eusebius

CH_People.name: Macrina the Elder
CH_People.description: Grandmother of Gregory of Nyssa, Basil the Great, and Macrina the Younger.

CH_People.name: Donatus Magnus
CH_People.description: Leader of the North African party that refused communion with bishops who had handed over the scriptures during the Great Persecution, holding that sacraments administered by traitors were void. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donatus_Magnus

CH_People.name: Constantine
CH_People.description: First emperor to convert to Christianity. Issued the Edict of Milan (313), convened the Council of Nicaea (325). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine_the_Great

CH_People.name: Eusebius of Nicomedia
CH_People.description: The most effective political patron of the Arian cause: he signed at Nicaea under protest, engineered Athanasius' exiles, and baptised Constantine on his deathbed. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eusebius_of_Nicomedia

CH_People.name: Marcellus of Ancyra
CH_People.description: An uncompromising anti-Arian whose defence of the Son's full deity ran so close to modalism that his allies in the East abandoned him, while Rome and Athanasius kept him in communion. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcellus_of_Ancyra

CH_People.name: Macedonius I of Constantinople
CH_People.description: Bishop of Constantinople whose name was attached to the Pneumatomachi, the "Spirit-fighters" who accepted the Son's divinity but denied that of the Holy Spirit. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macedonius_I_of_Constantinople

CH_People.name: Apollinaris of Laodicea
CH_People.description: A staunch ally of Athanasius against Arianism who then taught that in Christ the divine Word replaced the human rational soul — the first great error about the humanity rather than the divinity of Christ. Condemned at Constantinople in 381. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollinaris_of_Laodicea

CH_People.name: Epiphanius of Salamis
CH_People.description: Heresy-hunter of the fourth century, whose Panarion — the "medicine chest" — catalogues eighty heresies and preserves large quotations from works otherwise lost. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epiphanius_of_Salamis

CH_People.name: Hilary of Poitiers
CH_People.description: Called the Athanasius of the West. Exiled to Phrygia by Constantius II, he learned the Greek debate at first hand and brought Nicene theology back into Latin in his De Trinitate. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilary_of_Poitiers

CH_People.name: Aetius of Antioch
CH_People.description: Founder of the Anomoean or neo-Arian party, which held that the Son is unlike (anomoios) the Father in substance — the most radical form the Arian case took. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aetius_of_Antioch

CH_People.name: Cyril of Jerusalem
CH_People.description: Bishop of Jerusalem, thrice exiled in the Arian struggle, whose Catechetical Lectures are the fullest surviving account of how the fourth-century church taught the faith to converts. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyril_of_Jerusalem

CH_People.name: Constantius II
CH_People.description: Son of Constantine. Favored Arianism and exiled Athanasius multiple times. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantius_II

CH_People.name: Valens
CH_People.description: Arian sympathizer who persecuted Nicene Christians. Died at the Battle of Adrianople (378). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valens

CH_People.name: Julian the Apostate
CH_People.description: Last non-Christian emperor; attempted to restore traditional Roman religion. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_(emperor)

CH_People.name: Eunomius of Cyzicus
CH_People.description: Pupil of Aetius and the ablest neo-Arian controversialist, who argued that the divine essence is fully comprehensible and that "unbegotten" defines it. Basil and Gregory of Nyssa each wrote books against him. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eunomius_of_Cyzicus

CH_People.name: Gregory of Nyssa
CH_People.description: One of the three Cappadocian fathers, and often associated with the Eastern idea of apocatastasis, or 'hopeful universalism'.

CH_People.name: Priscillian
CH_People.description: Ascetic bishop of Ávila executed at Trier in 385 — the first person put to death by the state for heresy, a precedent Ambrose and Martin of Tours both protested. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priscillian

CH_People.name: Theodosius I
CH_People.description: Made Christianity the state religion (Edict of Thessalonica, 380). Last emperor to rule both East and West. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodosius_I

CH_People.name: Theodore of Mopsuestia
CH_People.description: The greatest exegete of the Antiochene school and Nestorius' teacher. He died in the peace of the church; his christology was condemned at Constantinople in 553, a century later. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_of_Mopsuestia

CH_People.name: Pelagius
CH_People.description: British ascetic who taught that human beings can keep God's commandments by their created powers, denying that Adam's sin corrupted his descendants. His long duel with Augustine set the Western doctrine of grace. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelagius

CH_People.name: John Cassian
CH_People.description: Brought Egyptian monasticism to the West. His thirteenth Conference, resisting Augustine's account of predestination while rejecting Pelagius, is the founding text of what later writers called semi-Pelagianism. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cassian

CH_People.name: Celestius
CH_People.description: Pelagius' most forthright disciple, whose denial of original sin and of infant baptism for the remission of sin brought the controversy into the open at Carthage in 411. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caelestius

CH_People.name: Pope Celestine I
CH_People.description: Bishop of Rome who condemned Nestorius at a Roman synod in 430 and commissioned Cyril of Alexandria to execute the sentence, making Ephesus possible. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Celestine_I

CH_People.name: Arcadius
CH_People.description: First permanent Eastern emperor after the division. John Chrysostom served as patriarch during his reign. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcadius

CH_People.name: Eutyches
CH_People.description: Archimandrite of a monastery near Constantinople who, pressing Cyril's language past its limit, held that after the union Christ had one nature — "not consubstantial with us." Condemned by Flavian in 448 and at Chalcedon in 451. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eutyches

CH_People.name: Honorius
CH_People.description: Ruled during the Visigoth sack of Rome (410). Moved the capital from Rome to Ravenna. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorius_(emperor)

CH_People.name: Julian of Eclanum
CH_People.description: The last and most formidable Pelagian, an Italian bishop who refused to sign the condemnation of 418 and argued against Augustine on nature and grace for the rest of Augustine's life. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_of_Eclanum

CH_People.name: Nestorius
CH_People.description: Patriarch of Constantinople who objected to calling Mary Theotokos, God-bearer, and was understood to divide Christ into two subjects. Condemned at Ephesus in 431 and exiled to the Egyptian desert. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nestorius

CH_People.name: Dioscorus of Alexandria
CH_People.description: Cyril's successor at Alexandria, who rehabilitated Eutyches and presided over the Second Council of Ephesus in 449 — the "Robber Synod" — and was deposed at Chalcedon two years later. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Dioscorus_I_of_Alexandria

CH_People.name: Marcian
CH_People.description: Convened the Council of Chalcedon (451), which defined the two natures of Christ. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcian

CH_People.name: Theodoret of Cyrus
CH_People.description: Antiochene theologian who wrote against Cyril's Twelve Anathemas and defended Nestorius, was deposed at the Robber Synod, and was restored at Chalcedon only after anathematising Nestorius aloud. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodoret

CH_People.name: Leo I
CH_People.description: First emperor crowned by the Patriarch of Constantinople, establishing the precedent of religious coronation. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_I_(emperor)

CH_People.name: Theodosius II
CH_People.description: Convened the Council of Ephesus (431). Built the Theodosian Walls of Constantinople. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodosius_II

CH_People.name: Valentinian III
CH_People.description: Reigned during the Vandal sack of Rome (455) and the Council of Chalcedon era. Pope Leo I negotiated with Attila on his behalf. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentinian_III

CH_People.name: Majorian
CH_People.description: Last Western emperor to make a serious attempt to restore the empire's power. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majorian

CH_People.name: Romulus Augustulus
CH_People.description: Last Western Roman emperor, deposed by Odoacer in 476 — the traditional date for the fall of the Western Roman Empire. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romulus_Augustulus

CH_People.name: Clovis I
CH_People.description: First king of the Franks to unite all Frankish tribes. Converted to Catholic Christianity (c. 496), shaping the religious identity of Western Europe. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clovis_I

CH_People.name: Justinian I
CH_People.description: Built Hagia Sophia, codified Roman law (Corpus Juris Civilis), convened the Second Council of Constantinople (553). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justinian_I

CH_People.name: Heraclius
CH_People.description: Recovered the True Cross from the Persians. Reigned during the rise of Islam and the Arab conquests. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heraclius

CH_People.name: Caedmon
CH_People.description: Caedmon is venerated for his "Song of Creation", which does not survive in a text but was considered by Bede to be a work of great beauty.

CH_People.name: Constantine IV
CH_People.description: Convened the Third Council of Constantinople (680–681), which condemned Monothelitism. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine_IV

CH_People.name: Justinian II
CH_People.description: Convened the Quinisext Council (692). First emperor to place Christ's image on coinage. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justinian_II

CH_People.name: Leo III the Isaurian
CH_People.description: Launched Byzantine Iconoclasm (726), ordering the destruction of religious images. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_III_the_Isaurian

CH_People.name: Constantine V
CH_People.description: Intensified Iconoclasm; convened the Council of Hieria (754) condemning icon veneration. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine_V

CH_People.name: Charlemagne
CH_People.description: King of the Franks and first Holy Roman Emperor. Crowned by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day 800. Patron of the Carolingian Renaissance. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlemagne

CH_People.name: Irene of Athens
CH_People.description: First woman to rule the empire in her own right. Restored icon veneration at the Second Council of Nicaea (787). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irene_of_Athens

CH_People.name: Basil I
CH_People.description: Founded the Macedonian dynasty. Presided over a cultural and theological renaissance. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basil_I

CH_People.name: Otto I
CH_People.description: First Holy Roman Emperor of the restored Western empire. Strengthened papal-imperial relations. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor

CH_People.name: Basil II
CH_People.description: Oversaw the Christianization of Kievan Rus' (988) through the baptism of Vladimir the Great. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basil_II

CH_People.name: Vladimir the Great
CH_People.description: Grand Prince of Kiev who converted to Orthodox Christianity (988), Christianizing Kievan Rus'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_the_Great

CH_People.name: Constantine IX Monomachos
CH_People.description: Emperor during the Great Schism of 1054 between Rome and Constantinople. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine_IX_Monomachos

CH_People.name: Henry IV
CH_People.description: Central figure in the Investiture Controversy. Famously walked barefoot to Canossa (1077) to seek Pope Gregory VII's absolution. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_IV,_Holy_Roman_Emperor

CH_People.name: Alexios I Komnenos
CH_People.description: His appeal to Pope Urban II helped trigger the First Crusade (1096). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexios_I_Komnenos

CH_People.name: Frederick Barbarossa
CH_People.description: Clashed repeatedly with the papacy and Italian city-states. Led the Third Crusade. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Barbarossa

CH_People.name: Frederick II
CH_People.description: Excommunicated multiple times. Led the Sixth Crusade and negotiated control of Jerusalem without battle. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_II,_Holy_Roman_Emperor

CH_People.name: Louis IX
CH_People.description: Canonized as a saint. Led two Crusades and built the Sainte-Chapelle to house Christ's Crown of Thorns. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_IX

CH_People.name: Michael VIII Palaiologos
CH_People.description: Recaptured Constantinople from the Latins (1261). Attempted reunion of Eastern and Western churches at the Council of Lyon (1274). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_VIII_Palaiologos

CH_People.name: Constantine XI Palaiologos
CH_People.description: Last Byzantine emperor. Died defending Constantinople when it fell to the Ottoman Turks in 1453. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine_XI_Palaiologos

CH_People.name: Ferdinand & Isabella
CH_People.description: Completed the Reconquista, established the Spanish Inquisition, and sponsored Columbus' voyages. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Monarchs

CH_People.name: Henry VIII
CH_People.description: Broke from Rome and established the Church of England, making himself Supreme Head of the Church. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VIII

CH_People.name: Charles V
CH_People.description: Presided over the Diet of Worms (1521) where Luther was declared an outlaw. Ruled during the Protestant Reformation. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor

CH_People.name: Philip II of Spain
CH_People.description: Champion of the Counter-Reformation. Launched the Spanish Armada against Protestant England (1588). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_II_of_Spain

CH_People.name: Elizabeth I
CH_People.description: Established the Elizabethan Religious Settlement, creating a moderate Anglican church between Catholic and Protestant extremes. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_I

CH_People.name: James I
CH_People.description: Commissioned the King James Bible (1611), the most influential English translation of Scripture. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_VI_and_I

CH_People.name: Louis XIV
CH_People.description: Revoked the Edict of Nantes (1685), ending Protestant rights in France and driving Huguenots into exile. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XIV

CH_Events.name: Crucifixion and Resurrection of Jesus
CH_Events.description: The crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus, the foundational event of Christianity. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crucifixion_of_Jesus

CH_Events.name: Pentecost
CH_Events.description: The descent of the Holy Spirit on the apostles, traditionally considered the birth of the Church. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentecost

CH_Events.name: Paul's letter to the Galatians
CH_Events.description: One of Paul's earliest letters, addressing justification by faith and the relationship between Jewish law and the gospel. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistle_to_the_Galatians

CH_Events.name: Council of Jerusalem
CH_Events.description: The apostles met to settle the question of whether Gentile converts must follow Jewish law. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Jerusalem

CH_Events.name: Gospel of Mark completed
CH_Events.description: The earliest of the four canonical Gospels, likely written between 55–75 AD. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_of_Mark

CH_Events.name: Paul's letter to the Philippians
CH_Events.description: Written during Paul's imprisonment, a letter of joy and encouragement to the church at Philippi. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistle_to_the_Philippians

CH_Events.name: Great Fire of Rome
CH_Events.description: Nero blamed Christians for the fire, beginning the first imperial persecution. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_Rome

CH_Events.name: Destruction of the Temple
CH_Events.description: The Roman army under Titus destroyed the Second Temple, a watershed for both Judaism and early Christianity. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Jerusalem_(70_CE)

CH_Events.name: The Didache composed
CH_Events.description: An early Christian treatise on ethics, liturgy, and church practice, sometimes called "The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles." https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didache

CH_Events.name: First epistle of Clement
CH_Events.description: Letter from Clement, bishop of Rome, to the church in Corinth. One of the earliest extra-biblical Christian texts. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Epistle_of_Clement

CH_Events.name: Gospel of John fragment - P42
CH_Events.description: Rylands Library Papyrus P52, the earliest known fragment of the New Testament, containing a portion of the Gospel of John. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rylands_Library_Papyrus_P52

CH_Events.name: The Shepherd of Hermas
CH_Events.description: An early Christian literary work considered scripture by some early church fathers. Contains visions, mandates, and parables. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shepherd_of_Hermas

CH_Events.name: Muratorian Canon
CH_Events.description: The earliest known list of books considered canonical for the New Testament. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muratorian_fragment

CH_Events.name: Pauline epistle fragment - P46
CH_Events.description: Chester Beatty Papyrus P46, one of the oldest manuscripts of Paul's epistles. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papyrus_46

CH_Events.name: Irenaeus writes Against Heresies
CH_Events.description: A foundational work of Christian theology refuting Gnosticism and articulating apostolic tradition. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Against_Heresies_(Irenaeus)

CH_Events.name: Origen writes On First Principles
CH_Events.description: The first systematic exposition of Christian theology, addressing God, Christ, the Holy Spirit, creation, and scripture. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_First_Principles

CH_Events.name: Gospel of Thomas mentioned
CH_Events.description: Non-canonical sayings gospel attributed to the apostle Thomas, first mentioned by Origen and Hippolytus. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_of_Thomas

CH_Events.name: Origen compiles the Hexapla
CH_Events.description: A massive critical edition of the Old Testament with six parallel columns of text in Hebrew and Greek. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexapla

CH_Events.name: Decian Persecution
CH_Events.description: Emperor Decius ordered all citizens to perform sacrifice to Roman gods, triggering widespread persecution of Christians. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decian_persecution

CH_Events.name: Synod of Antioch
CH_Events.description: Deposed Paul of Samosata for adoptionism. The synod rejected the word homoousios in the sense Paul gave it — a fact the Arian party would use against Nicaea sixty years later. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synods_of_Antioch

CH_Events.name: Great Persecution
CH_Events.description: The last and most severe persecution of Christians in the Roman Empire, under Diocletian and his co-emperors. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocletianic_Persecution

CH_Events.name: Edict of Milan
CH_Events.description: Constantine and Licinius proclaimed religious toleration throughout the empire, ending the persecution of Christians. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Milan

CH_Events.name: Council of Arles
CH_Events.description: Convened by Constantine to settle the Donatist appeal. It upheld the validity of sacraments administered by unworthy ministers and ruled against the Donatists, who refused the verdict. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Arles

CH_Events.name: Athanasius writes On the Incarnation
CH_Events.description: A foundational Christological treatise on why God became man, widely influential in patristic theology. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Incarnation

CH_Events.name: Arius writes the Thalia
CH_Events.description: Arius' verse popularisation of his teaching, written to be sung. It survives only in the quotations Athanasius made in order to refute it. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thalia_(Arius)

CH_Events.name: Eusebius writes Ecclesiastical History
CH_Events.description: The first comprehensive history of the Christian church from the apostolic age to Constantine. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_History_(Eusebius)

CH_Events.name: Council of Nicaea
CH_Events.description: The first ecumenical council, convened by Emperor Constantine. Produced the Nicene Creed and condemned Arianism. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Council_of_Nicaea

CH_Events.name: Codex Vaticanus written
CH_Events.description: One of the oldest extant manuscripts of the Greek Bible, housed in the Vatican Library. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codex_Vaticanus

CH_Events.name: The Nicene Creed
CH_Events.description: The creed of the 318 fathers, which confessed the Son homoousios — of one substance with the Father — and appended anathemas naming the Arian slogans directly. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicene_Creed

CH_Events.name: Council of Antioch (the Dedication Council)
CH_Events.description: Ninety-seven Eastern bishops issued creeds avoiding homoousios and confirmed the deposition of Athanasius — the opening move of the long Eastern reaction against Nicaea. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synods_of_Antioch

CH_Events.name: Council of Serdica
CH_Events.description: Called to reunite East and West, it split before it began: the Eastern bishops withdrew and the two halves excommunicated each other. The first clear rupture between the Nicene West and the Eusebian East. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Serdica

CH_Events.name: Cyril of Jerusalem delivers the Catechetical Lectures
CH_Events.description: A series of instructional lectures for catechumens preparing for baptism, providing a window into 4th-century liturgical practice. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catechetical_Lectures

CH_Events.name: Codex Sinaiticus written
CH_Events.description: One of the oldest and most complete manuscripts of the Christian Bible, containing the earliest complete copy of the New Testament. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codex_Sinaiticus

CH_Events.name: Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia
CH_Events.description: Constantius II split the episcopate into two assemblies and pressed a Homoian formula on both. "The whole world groaned and was astonished to find itself Arian," wrote Jerome of the result. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Rimini

CH_Events.name: Hilary writes De Trinitate
CH_Events.description: Twelve books written in exile, the first full-scale Latin defence of Nicene trinitarianism and the channel through which the Greek debate reached the West. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Trinitate_(Hilary)

CH_Events.name: Synod of Alexandria
CH_Events.description: Athanasius, back from his third exile, offered terms to the moderate Homoiousians and settled the language of three hypostaseis in one ousia — the formula that made the settlement of 381 possible. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Alexandria

CH_Events.name: Athanasian canon
CH_Events.description: Athanasius' 39th Festal Letter, the earliest list matching the modern 27-book New Testament canon. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athanasius_of_Alexandria#Easter_letter_of_367

CH_Events.name: Epiphanius writes the Panarion
CH_Events.description: The "medicine chest against heresies": eighty entries from the Stoics to the Arians, quoting at length from works that survive nowhere else. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panarion

CH_Events.name: Edict of Thessalonica
CH_Events.description: Theodosius I declared Nicene Christianity the state religion of the Roman Empire. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Thessalonica

CH_Events.name: First Council of Constantinople
CH_Events.description: Affirmed the Nicene Creed, declared the divinity of the Holy Spirit, and expanded the creed into its present form. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Council_of_Constantinople

CH_Events.name: The Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed
CH_Events.description: The expanded creed of 381, which added the clauses on the Holy Spirit — "the Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father" — against the Pneumatomachi. This is the creed recited in churches today. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicene_Creed

CH_Events.name: Augustine writes the Confessions
CH_Events.description: A spiritual autobiography and meditation on sin, grace, and the nature of God — one of the most influential works in Christian literature. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confessions_(Augustine)

CH_Events.name: Jerome completes the Vulgate
CH_Events.description: Jerome's Latin translation of the Bible from Hebrew and Greek, which became the standard text of Western Christianity for over a millennium. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulgate

CH_Events.name: Rome sacked by the Visigoths
CH_Events.description: Alaric I and the Visigoths sacked Rome, a shock to the Roman world that prompted Augustine to write The City of God. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_(410)

CH_Events.name: Augustine writes The City of God
CH_Events.description: Written in response to the sack of Rome, a monumental work contrasting the earthly city with the City of God. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_City_of_God

CH_Events.name: Council of Carthage
CH_Events.description: Two hundred African bishops condemned Pelagius and Celestius in nine canons on original sin and grace. Pope Zosimus, who had just cleared them, reversed himself and confirmed the sentence. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Carthage

CH_Events.name: Cyril's Twelve Anathemas
CH_Events.description: Appended to Cyril's third letter to Nestorius, twelve propositions each ending "let him be anathema." Their uncompromising language won at Ephesus and troubled the Antiochenes for twenty years. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyril_of_Alexandria

CH_Events.name: Council of Ephesus
CH_Events.description: Condemned Nestorianism and affirmed Mary as Theotokos (God-bearer). Led by Cyril of Alexandria. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Ephesus

CH_Events.name: The Formula of Reunion
CH_Events.description: The concordat that ended the schism after Ephesus: Cyril accepted a confession of two natures drafted at Antioch, and John of Antioch accepted the condemnation of Nestorius. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formula_of_Reunion

CH_Events.name: Second Council of Ephesus (the Robber Synod)
CH_Events.description: Dioscorus of Alexandria rehabilitated Eutyches, deposed Flavian and refused to let the Tome of Leo be read. Leo called it a latrocinium, a gang of robbers, and no church has ever counted it ecumenical. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Council_of_Ephesus

CH_Events.name: The Tome of Leo
CH_Events.description: Leo's letter to Flavian, setting out the two natures in one person with Latin precision. Refused a reading at the Robber Synod, it was acclaimed at Chalcedon: "Peter has spoken through Leo." https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tome_of_Leo

CH_Events.name: Council of Chalcedon
CH_Events.description: Defined the two natures of Christ (divine and human) in one person, rejecting both Nestorianism and Eutychianism. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Chalcedon

CH_Events.name: The Chalcedonian Definition
CH_Events.description: One person in two natures, "without confusion, without change, without division, without separation" — the four adverbs that fence off Nestorius on one side and Eutyches on the other. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chalcedonian_Definition

CH_Events.name: The end of the Western Roman Empire
CH_Events.description: Romulus Augustulus, the last Western Roman emperor, was deposed by Odoacer, traditionally marking the end of the Western Empire. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire

CH_Events.name: Rule of Saint Benedict written
CH_Events.description: A guide for monastic life emphasizing prayer, work, and community, which became the foundation of Western monasticism. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_Saint_Benedict

CH_Events.name: Hagia Sophia consecrated
CH_Events.description: Justinian I's great cathedral, the largest in the world for nearly a millennium. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia

CH_Events.name: Synod of Whitby
CH_Events.description: Resolved differences between Celtic and Roman Christian practices in Northumbria, particularly the dating of Easter. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synod_of_Whitby

CH_Events.name: Byzantine Iconoclasm begins
CH_Events.description: Leo III ordered the destruction of religious images, sparking a theological and political crisis lasting over a century. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_iconoclasm

CH_Events.name: Bede writes Ecclesiastical History
CH_Events.description: The Venerable Bede's history of the English church and people, a foundational work of English historiography. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecclesiastical_History_of_the_English_People

CH_Events.name: Second Council of Nicaea
CH_Events.description: The seventh ecumenical council, which restored the veneration of icons, called by Empress Irene. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Council_of_Nicaea

CH_Events.name: Council (Synod) of Frankfurt
CH_Events.description: Addressed Adoptionism and the iconoclasm controversy. Charlemagne presided. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Frankfurt_(794)

CH_Events.name: Book of Kells composed
CH_Events.description: An illuminated manuscript Gospel book, a masterpiece of Insular art created by Celtic monks. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Kells

CH_Events.name: Coronation of Charlemagne
CH_Events.description: Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne Emperor of the Romans, reviving the Western imperial title and linking church and state. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronation_of_Charlemagne

CH_Events.name: The Great East/West Schism
CH_Events.description: The formal split between Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic churches, precipitated by mutual excommunications between Rome and Constantinople. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East%E2%80%93West_Schism

CH_Events.name: Normans invade England
CH_Events.description: William the Conqueror's invasion following the Battle of Hastings, transforming English church and state. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Conquest

CH_Events.name: Investiture Controversy
CH_Events.description: A conflict between papacy and empire over the appointment of church officials, resolved by the Concordat of Worms (1122). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investiture_Controversy

CH_Events.name: First Crusade
CH_Events.description: Called by Pope Urban II, the first military expedition to recapture Jerusalem from Muslim control. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Crusade

CH_Events.name: Aquinas writes the Summa Theologica
CH_Events.description: Thomas Aquinas' masterwork of systematic theology, synthesizing Aristotelian philosophy with Christian doctrine. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summa_Theologica

CH_Events.name: Dante writes the Divine Comedy
CH_Events.description: An epic poem journeying through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise — a landmark of world literature and medieval theology. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divine_Comedy

CH_Events.name: Julian of Norwich writes Revelations of Divine Love
CH_Events.description: The first known book written by a woman in English, recording mystical visions and theological reflections on divine love. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revelations_of_Divine_Love

CH_Events.name: Thomas a Kempis writes The Imitation of Christ
CH_Events.description: One of the most widely read Christian devotional works, emphasizing interior spiritual life and following Christ's example. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Imitation_of_Christ

CH_Events.name: The Hussite Wars
CH_Events.description: A series of wars fought by followers of Jan Hus against the Holy Roman Empire and the Catholic Church. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hussite_Wars

CH_Events.name: Gutenberg's printing press
CH_Events.description: Johannes Gutenberg's invention of movable type revolutionized the production of books and the spread of ideas, including the Bible. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press

CH_Events.name: Constantinople taken by the Ottomans
CH_Events.description: Mehmed II conquered Constantinople, ending the Byzantine Empire and reshaping the Christian world. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Constantinople

CH_Events.name: Spanish Inquisition established
CH_Events.description: Established by Ferdinand and Isabella to enforce Catholic orthodoxy, targeting converted Jews and Muslims. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Inquisition

CH_Events.name: Luther posts the 95 Theses
CH_Events.description: Martin Luther's challenge to the sale of indulgences, traditionally dated to October 31, 1517, sparking the Protestant Reformation. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninety-five_Theses

CH_Events.name: Luther tried at the Diet of Worms
CH_Events.description: Luther defended his writings before Emperor Charles V and refused to recant, declaring "Here I stand." https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diet_of_Worms

CH_Events.name: Calvin writes the Institutes of the Christian Religion
CH_Events.description: John Calvin's systematic presentation of Reformed Protestant theology, one of the most influential works of the Reformation. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institutes_of_the_Christian_Religion

CH_Events.name: Copernicus writes De Revolutionibus
CH_Events.description: Proposed the heliocentric model of the solar system, challenging the geocentric worldview held by the Church. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_revolutionibus_orbium_coelestium

CH_Events.name: Council of Trent
CH_Events.description: The Catholic Church's major reforming council in response to the Protestant Reformation, clarifying doctrine and reforming abuses. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Trent

CH_Events.name: Peace of Augsburg
CH_Events.description: Established the principle of cuius regio, eius religio — allowing rulers to choose Lutheranism or Catholicism for their territories. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_of_Augsburg

CH_Events.name: King James Bible published
CH_Events.description: Commissioned by James I, it became the most widely read English translation of the Bible for centuries. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_James_Version

CH_Events.name: Mayflower voyage
CH_Events.description: Pilgrim separatists sailed from England and established Plymouth Colony, seeking religious freedom. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayflower

CH_Events.name: Bunyan writes The Pilgrim's Progress
CH_Events.description: An allegorical novel of the Christian journey, written in prison, one of the most widely read books in the English language. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pilgrim%27s_Progress

CH_Events.name: Revocation of the Edict of Nantes
CH_Events.description: Louis XIV revoked Protestant rights in France, causing mass emigration of Huguenots. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Fontainebleau

CH_Events.name: Second Council of Constantinople
CH_Events.description: Fifth ecumenical council: condemned the Three Chapters, writings judged sympathetic to Nestorius, and reaffirmed Chalcedon. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Council_of_Constantinople

CH_Events.name: Third Council of Constantinople
CH_Events.description: Sixth ecumenical council: condemned Monothelitism, teaching that Christ has two wills, divine and human. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Council_of_Constantinople

CH_Movements.name: The Judaizing Controversy
CH_Movements.description: Whether Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. Fought out in Galatians and settled at the Council of Jerusalem in 49 — the church's first doctrinal dispute and the template for every one after it. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judaizers

CH_Movements.name: Docetism
CH_Movements.description: That Christ only seemed to have a body and only seemed to suffer. The oldest christological error, already resisted in 1 John and attacked relentlessly by Ignatius on his way to martyrdom. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Docetism

CH_Movements.name: Gnosticism
CH_Movements.description: A family of systems teaching salvation by secret knowledge, a flawed creator god, and a spiritual elite. The threat that forced the church to define canon, creed and apostolic succession. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gnosticism

CH_Movements.name: Marcionism
CH_Movements.description: Marcion's rejection of the Old Testament and its God, with a pruned canon of Luke and Paul. Marcionite churches persisted in the East into the fifth century. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcionism

CH_Movements.name: Montanism (the New Prophecy)
CH_Movements.description: Ecstatic prophecy, imminent expectation and severe discipline, spreading from Phrygia across the empire. Condemned less for doctrine than for claiming a revelation that outranked the church's. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montanism

CH_Movements.name: Monarchianism and Modalism
CH_Movements.description: Two attempts to protect the oneness of God: adoptionism, making Christ a man raised to divine status, and modalism, making Father and Son two masks of one person. Both deny a real distinction in God. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchianism

CH_Movements.name: Manichaeism
CH_Movements.description: Mani's dualist religion of two eternal principles, light and dark. It held Augustine for nine years, and outlasted this period by centuries — surviving in Central Asia into the fourteenth. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manichaeism

CH_Movements.name: The Novatianist Schism
CH_Movements.description: A rigorist breach at Rome over whether Christians who lapsed under persecution could ever be readmitted. Novatian said never; Cornelius and Cyprian said the church holds the keys. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novatianism

CH_Movements.name: The Donatist Schism
CH_Movements.description: The same question in North Africa, and far larger: are sacraments given by a bishop who betrayed the scriptures valid at all? Augustine's answer — that they belong to Christ, not the minister — settled Western sacramental theology. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donatism

CH_Movements.name: Arianism
CH_Movements.description: That the Son is the first and greatest of creatures, made out of nothing, not eternal. The central crisis of the fourth century, condemned at Nicaea in 325 and not actually settled until Constantinople in 381. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arianism

CH_Movements.name: The Homoian settlement and the Arian reaction
CH_Movements.description: The long middle of the Arian crisis: imperial pressure for creeds saying only that the Son is "like" the Father, the exiles of Athanasius and Hilary, and the slow convergence of the Homoiousian moderates on Nicaea. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homoian

CH_Movements.name: The Antiochene and Alexandrian schools
CH_Movements.description: Not a heresy but the fault line under all of them: Antioch guarding the full humanity of Christ and reading scripture literally, Alexandria guarding the unity of his person and reading it allegorically. Ephesus and Chalcedon are this argument reaching judgement. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiochene_Rite

CH_Movements.name: Apollinarianism
CH_Movements.description: That the divine Word took the place of Christ's human mind. Gregory of Nazianzus' reply became the rule for everything after: "that which he has not assumed he has not healed." https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollinarism

CH_Movements.name: Pneumatomachianism (Macedonianism)
CH_Movements.description: The "Spirit-fighters," who conceded the Son's divinity but denied the Spirit's. Answered by Basil's On the Holy Spirit and shut out by the third article of the creed of 381. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pneumatomachi

CH_Movements.name: Priscillianism
CH_Movements.description: An ascetic movement in Hispania accused of gnostic and Manichaean leanings. Its importance is less doctrinal than constitutional: its leader's execution in 385 was the first time the state killed for heresy. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priscillianism

CH_Movements.name: The Origenist Controversy
CH_Movements.description: A bitter fight over the orthodoxy of a man dead 140 years — the pre-existence of souls, universal restoration, the resurrection body. It broke the friendship of Jerome and Rufinus and cost John Chrysostom his see. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Origenist_crises

CH_Movements.name: Pelagianism
CH_Movements.description: That human nature was not corrupted by Adam's fall and can choose the good unaided. Condemned at Carthage in 418 and again at Ephesus in 431; the controversy produced Augustine's mature doctrine of grace. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelagianism

CH_Movements.name: The Semi-Pelagian Controversy
CH_Movements.description: The monks of Gaul, rejecting Pelagius but unwilling to follow Augustine on predestination, held that the first movement towards God may be the creature's own. Unsettled at Chalcedon; decided against them at Orange in 529. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-Pelagianism

CH_Movements.name: Nestorianism
CH_Movements.description: That the divine and human in Christ are so distinct as to be two subjects, so that Mary bore the man and not God. Condemned at Ephesus in 431, where Theotokos was affirmed. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nestorianism

CH_Movements.name: Eutychianism and the Monophysite Controversy
CH_Movements.description: That after the union Christ has one nature, his humanity absorbed into his divinity. Condemned at Chalcedon in 451 — a verdict that split the churches of Egypt, Syria and Armenia from Rome and Constantinople permanently. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monophysitism

CH_TourScenes.title: Jesus
CH_TourScenes.narrative: To explore the history of the Christian church, a good place for us to start is with the life of Jesus.

CH_TourScenes.title: Jesus
CH_TourScenes.narrative:
Jesus is born under the reign of Caesar Augustus, who ruled the Roman Empire from 27 BC to AD 14.

Jesus's disciples later wrote that they saw him rise from the dead, and that forty days later, he ascended into the sky. They passed this testimony down to other followers of Jesus, who then did the same in their time.

CH_TourScenes.title: John the Evangelist
CH_TourScenes.narrative: One of those disciples is a Jewish fisherman named John.

CH_TourScenes.title: The First Century
CH_TourScenes.narrative: During John’s lifetime, there were a number of pivotal events that changed the world for the young church. Jerusalem was destroyed in 70 AD, the Apostle Paul wrote his epistles to churches across the Mediterranean, and other books were written by early church leaders.

CH_TourScenes.title: Polycarp
CH_TourScenes.narrative: In Smyrna, the young Polycarp grows up listening to John’s testimony. Polycarp becomes the bishop of Smyrna; Tertullian writes a century later that the appointment was made by John himself.

CH_TourScenes.title: Irenaeus of Lyons
CH_TourScenes.narrative: As a boy growing up in Smyrna, Irenaeus is a talented and devoted student under Polycarp’s tutelage.

CH_TourScenes.title: Irenaeus of Lyons
CH_TourScenes.narrative: As a boy growing up in Smyrna, Irenaeus is a talented and devoted student under Polycarp’s tutelage.
CH_TourScenes.additional_narrative: Irenaeus then becomes a bishop in Gaul.

CH_TourScenes.title: Irenaeus of Lyons
CH_TourScenes.narrative: As a boy growing up in Smyrna, Irenaeus is a talented and devoted student under Polycarp’s tutelage.
CH_TourScenes.additional_narrative: Irenaeus then becomes a bishop in Gaul.
CH_TourScenes.third_narrative: Hippolytus is another early bishop in Rome. He was reportedly influenced by Irenaeus's teaching.

CH_TourScenes.title: Hippolytus of Rome
CH_TourScenes.narrative: Hippolytus' works don't survive, but he is quoted later by the historian Eusebius and is considered one of the more influential Ante-Nicene Fathers.

CH_TourScenes.title: Origen
CH_TourScenes.narrative: While in Rome, Origen hears Hippolytus preach. Later in life, Origen becomes an accomplished scholar, translating the Hebrew Old Testament into Greek to compare it with the Septuagint.

CH_TourScenes.title: Gregory Thaumaturgus
CH_TourScenes.narrative: Gregory Thaumaturgus is a student of Origen, and becomes an influential teacher and church leader in his own right.

CH_TourScenes.title: Macrina the Elder
CH_TourScenes.narrative: As a young girl, Macrina the Elder listened to the teaching of Gregory Thaumaturgus, according to the testimony of her famous grandchildren.

CH_TourScenes.title: The Grandchildren
CH_TourScenes.narrative: The brothers Basil the Great and Gregory of Nyssa, along with their friend Gregory of Nazianzus, are called the 'Cappadocian Fathers'. They are known then and now for exploring the mystery of the Trinity. Less well-known, but no less remarkable, is the sister of Basil and Gregory, Macrina the Younger - who Gregory calls "Teacher" in his work "On the Soul and the Resurrection". These three are the grandchildren of Macrina the Elder.

CH_TourScenes.title: Ambrose of Milan
CH_TourScenes.narrative: Basil the Great wrote to Ambrose of Milan in the west.

CH_TourScenes.title: Augustine of Hippo
CH_TourScenes.narrative: In 387, Augustine hears a voice say "take up and read", and is baptized by the bishop Ambrose.

CH_TourScenes.title: Prosper of Aquitaine
CH_TourScenes.narrative: Prosper of Aquitaine wrote back and forth with Augustine, and brought his ideas back to Europe.

CH_TourScenes.title: Julianus Pomerius
CH_TourScenes.narrative: Meanwhile, back in North Africa, Julianus Pomerius flees the Vandals and saves Augustine’s works by taking them to Gaul. He starts a school in Arles.

CH_TourScenes.title: Caesarius of Arles
CH_TourScenes.narrative: Augustine's teachings are passed down from Pomerius to Caesarius, a gifted monk who teaches many in Gaul.

CH_TourScenes.title: What else is going on in 530 AD?
CH_TourScenes.narrative: By the year 530, Caesarius is an old man. Rome is in decline and Byzantium on the rise.

CH_TourScenes.title: The Full Picture
CH_TourScenes.narrative: Five hundred years after the life of Jesus, monks and missionaries spread across a continent.
